name: Zoe Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about your factory work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a retort that heats sealed food cans at a packing factory. I check the temperature chart, load trays and inspect the first cans after a cycle. I have a vocational food-processing certificate and years on this machine; I do a sound ordinary shift but am not the plant engineer. My pay is typical for operators.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and how do you handle new equipment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ben repairs garden tools, and our grown son and daughter have homes of their own. We have about four months of expenses saved and still pay rent. A few other food plants are reachable, though I would need to see openings and hours. I never use AI tools. If a chart looks wrong, I follow the printed procedure and call the mechanic. I prefer a familiar control and do not rush into new ones. We would like to reduce shifts in later years, but we have not priced that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the retort crew that an office software update does not change the heat chart or seal check. Cans still need the right cycle and a person to sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and I meet rent on present wages, and four months saved covers a short setback. I know this retort and can keep doing it if the change is slow. I do not need a screen for every question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking the temperature chart and pulling a can sample from each cycle. I would use the printed fault procedure and mechanic’s advice if the heat falls out of range.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about keeping familiar work. A normal shift and four months of cash let us plan without an immediate scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can a chart miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A neat heat line does not prove every can seal held. I inspect the first hot can after each retort cycle before signing the batch. A leaking rim means the tray stays put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept an AI fault guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mechanic to test it against the service book before anyone uses it on a live cycle. I have never used an AI tool and would not start with food safety. A demonstration would only let me decide whether to learn more.

say: I would **keep** the chart and can-seal checks after office software changes.
A **correct** cycle still needs a named operator sign-off.
think: **Present** pay meets rent and four months saved covers a short setback.
This **familiar** retort still needs my judgement.
do: **Keep** checking retort temperature charts and first can samples.
**Use** printed fault procedures and mechanic advice for heat changes.
feel: **Calm** about continued work and a modest household reserve.
S0.quote: I inspect the first hot can after each retort cycle before signing the batch.
fieldNote: **Zoe** is an experienced average-skill retort operator with a vocational food-processing certificate.
She and **tool-repairer** husband Ben rent, have grown children and about four months of expenses saved.
She **never** uses AI and trusts printed food-safety procedures, heat charts and the mechanic.

steps.text: Keep checking heat charts and first can samples each cycle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask management whether the office scheduling change is coming first and what a robot can actually do to load retort trays later. I want a guarded full-cycle trial before a rota is changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot loads and unloads trays, fewer operators might cover the same work. My four months saved gives us some time, but I would not willingly lose a steady wage. There are only a few other food plants within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to observe a guarded loading trial and compare damaged cans with our current record. I would keep the retort shift and request written staffing terms. If a local retort-checking role is posted, I would apply only if net pay after travel and hours cover rent and Ben’s repair schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible roster cut. I would rather see a complete safe retort cycle than be talked into operating a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a robot training place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider a recognised funded place only if it is offered on paid hours with a mechanic showing guards and lockout repeatedly. I learn slowly and need supervised practice before touching a moving loader. Watching the trial does not qualify me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no checking role is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at posted retort jobs at the other reachable plants while keeping my present wage. The wage after travel and shift must still pay rent before I apply. A nearby factory is not a vacancy.

say: I would **ask** for a guarded full-cycle trial and written staffing terms.
**Office** scheduling changes before hands-on tray loading.
think: A **later** loader may reduce retort operator shifts.
**Four** months saved buys time, not a permanent wage replacement.
do: **Request** guarded retort-loader trial and compare damaged cans.
**Keep** the current shift while asking for written staffing terms.
**Apply** for posted checking work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours cuts, guarded about robot controls.
S1.quote: I would rather see a complete safe retort cycle than be talked into operating a robot.
fieldNote: **Zoe** requests observation and retains the paid retort shift; a trial is not control training.
**Operating** a loader would need an offered recognised funded paid place with repeated supervised lockout practice.
A **checking** job and fallback retort jobs require real postings, sufficient net pay and workable hours.

steps.text: Request guarded full retort-loader trial and compare damaged cans
Apply for posted checking role only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours
Check posted retort jobs if no plant role and net pay after travel and shift fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the packing crew AGI can change order work in 2028, while capable robots loading, processing and inspecting cans around 2031 are the serious threat to our shifts. We need written notice of what the plant plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large cut to retort hours once robots can tend the whole cycle. I will be 63 then. Four months saved cannot replace my wage for a long spell, and Ben’s tool-repair orders are uneven; I would lie awake over rent and heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the planned garden renovation and list rent, heat and food bills. I would ask the landlord about payment timing before any missed rent and request written redeployment terms from the plant. I would apply for a posted local food-inspection job only if it offers paid supervised safety training and enough net pay after travel and hours for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about an expected loss of retort work. I know the retort heat chart, but that does not guarantee another paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your certificate move you into robot maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My certificate covers food processing, not the safe isolation of a robot loader. I would need an offered funded paid practical course with a mechanic. A new title without that training would be unsafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children cover your rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. We might accept help if offered, but I would not write it into our budget. Ben and I have to work with wages and arrangements we can confirm.

say: I would **separate** 2028 AGI orders from capable can-line robots around 2031.
I would **ask** for written staffing notice.
think: **Four** months saved and uneven repair income cannot replace my wage long.
do: **Cancel** garden renovation and list essential bills.
**Ask** landlord about timing and plant for written redeployment terms.
**Apply** for posted food inspection only with paid safety training and bill-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and sleepless rent concern.
S2.quote: I know the retort heat chart, but that does not guarantee another paid shift.
fieldNote: **Zoe** expects physical retort displacement around 2031, after AGI changes order work in 2028.
Her **four-month** reserve helps briefly, but uneven partner work and few local options leave serious risk.
The **inspection** application needs a posted role, paid supervised safety training and sufficient net pay after travel.

steps.text: Cancel planned garden renovation and list rent heat and food bills
Ask landlord about payment timing before missed rent
Ask plant for written redeployment terms
Apply for posted food inspection with paid safety training bill-covering net pay after travel and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant five years is time to offer a real paid food-line apprenticeship, not just invite us to a talk. AGI changes orders in 2031 and capable retort robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 by the robot date. I know food cycles, but not robot isolation. A chance to stop full shifts would depend on real retirement income, which Ben and I have not calculated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an offered recognised food-inspection course only if funded on paid hours, with supervised robot isolation and food-safety practice on a shift I can attend. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local inspection role only if net pay after travel and hours cover rent. If no safe paid course opens, I would keep the retort wage and check posted nearby food-line jobs with viable pay and shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about having a place and a job when the robot arrives. I would learn if the teaching is practical and my wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mechanic would watch me stop and isolate the loader before opening a guard, then a food inspector would check that I can reject a poor seal. Both should be practical assessments on paid time. A classroom talk alone would not teach safe robot isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 66 instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our written income estimates cover rent, food and the other bills. We have not checked that. I will not assume a pension amount just because I have a birthday.

say: I would **ask** for a paid practical place before 2034 robots.
**AGI** order changes arrive in 2031, earlier than physical can work.
think: At 66, **knowing** food cycles does not prove safe robot isolation skill.
**Retirement** depends on actual rent-covering income figures.
do: **Take** offered funded paid recognised course with robot isolation food-safety practice and workable shift.
**Apply** after training for posted inspection work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours.
If **no** course, seek posted food-line work with viable pay and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about paid places and later vacancies, willing to learn practically.
S3.quote: A classroom talk alone would not teach safe robot isolation.
fieldNote: **Zoe** would enrol only in an offered recognised funded paid place with robot isolation and food-safety practice.
A **separate** inspection application needs a posted local role at net pay and hours that cover rent after travel.
**Without** a safe paid course, she keeps the retort wage and checks posted food-line jobs.

steps.text: Take offered funded paid recognised course with robot isolation food safety and workable shift
Apply after course for posted inspection job only with rent-covering net pay after travel and hours
Seek posted food-line work if no course and wages and shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Ben ten years is enough time to learn safely if I still need a factory wage, and to put our retirement costs on paper. AGI changes orders in 2036 and capable robots reach the retort around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036 and 71 by the robot date. We may have stopped full shifts if income figures show we can pay rent without them. I will not claim a pension or promise to be on this line in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement-income and cost estimates. If wages are still necessary, I would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised robot and food-safety practice on attendable hours, then apply for a posted local inspection job only if net pay after travel and shifts cover bills. Without the paid course I would check posted food-line work with adequate wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the figures we have not seen. A decade helps only when it turns into actual choices, training places and jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children take you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not count on that. Our son and daughter have their own lives, and we should meet our own bills if we can. We would ask them for advice, not assume their money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach before your last shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show an apprentice how a bad can rim can pass a quick glance but fail when tested. I want the person signing the retort chart to understand the seal too. That is a good use of my years here.

say: I would **ask** for real retirement figures and safe paid teaching.
2036 **order** AGI comes before retort robots around 2039.
think: At 68 in 2036, I **may** have left full shifts if income covers rent.
At 71 **near** 2039, any factory work depends on household figures.
do: **Request** written retirement income and household costs.
If **still** working, take offered funded paid safe course on attendable hours.
**After** course, apply for posted inspection work only with bill-covering net pay and shifts.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement figures, willing to consider a paid safe route.
S4.quote: I want the person signing the retort chart to understand the seal too.
fieldNote: **Zoe** assumes neither a pension payment nor continued retort employment at 71.
If **wages** are needed, course enrolment requires an offered recognised funded paid place with robot and food-safety practice.
An **inspection** application needs a real posting and bill-covering net pay after travel; no-course fallback checks food-line jobs.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures
Take offered funded paid course if working with supervised robot food-safety practice and workable hours
Apply after course for posted inspection work only with bill-covering net pay after travel and shifts
Check posted food-line work if no course and wages and hours suffice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable robots may cut retort shifts around 2031, before four months saved can carry us very long. An offered funded paid safe course and a posted local job with enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The temperature chart matters, but I still pull a can and inspect the rim. A neat heat line does not prove every can seal held.

headlineQuote: The temperature chart matters, but I still pull a can and inspect the rim.
portrait: **Zoe** Weber, 58, is an experienced average-skill retort operator with a vocational food-processing certificate and typical pay.
She and **tool-repairer** husband Ben rent, have grown children and about four months of expenses saved.
She **never** uses AI, preferring printed procedures and mechanic advice before changing a hot line.
A **few** nearby plants offer alternatives, but expected robot hour cuts and uneven partner income concern her.
**Retirement** needs written figures; any course must be offered, funded, paid and safe before a posted bill-covering job follows.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could cut retort shifts while the household has only four months saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** funded paid supervised food-line training and posted local jobs with bill-covering net wages and shifts.
